msItem.incipit: She's dead nor were it fit she should live still

abstract.p: The poem is a brief elegy on an unnamed woman whose death is presented as fitting. She is said to have lived honourably and to have died only four years short of the “full age of man,” most likely the biblical lifespan of seventy years from Psalm 90:10, which would make her about sixty-six. Life beyond that point is described as a condition of trouble, disease, sorrow, and “restlese ease.” After her husband’s death, she lives only long enough to mourn him and dies within the year; the poem presents widowhood, especially the “widdow bedd,” as a form of torture from which death releases her.

lg.l: Shees deade; nor were itt fitt shee should be live still,
To feele the malice of old ages ill;
Shee had with honoure measured her lifes spann,
And lackt but fouer yeeres o’th’full age of man
Whate’s beyond that is trouble and disease,
A dying life, sorrow and restlese ease.
Nor would she longer live life her husband deade,
To seek the tortures of a widdow bedd,
Shee only grac’d him with a funerall teare
Liv’d but to mourne and died within the yeare.
